body.hook: Jazz started in New Orleans around 1900, mixing African rhythms, blues, ragtime and brass band music. Ever since, musicians have been saying the same thing: if it doesn't swing, it doesn't mean a thing.

study.title: Swing, Latin, Rock and the Blues
study.question: How do jazz musicians play in different styles and improvise?
study.passage:
Part 1, Three feels (15 minutes): Play the same B-flat concert scale three ways:
• Swing: long-short eighths, light accent on off-beats, "doo-BA" articulation.
• Latin (bossa nova or Afro-Cuban): straight, even eighths, smooth and laid back for bossa; crisp and driving for Afro-Cuban.
• Rock: straight eighths with heavy backbeat feel; play with energy on beats 2 and 4.
Part 2, 12-bar blues (10 minutes): Concert B-flat blues: | B♭7 | E♭7 | B♭7 | B♭7 | E♭7 | E♭7 | B♭7 | B♭7 | F7 | E♭7 | B♭7 | F7 |. Rhythm section comps; winds play the root of each chord on beat 1.
Part 3, Blues scale (10 minutes): Learn the concert B-flat blues scale: B♭, D♭, E♭, E, F, A♭. Play up and down in swing.
Part 4, Call and response (10 minutes): The teacher plays a two-bar idea; everyone copies. Then individuals answer with their own two bars.
Part 5, Solos (10 minutes): Each player improvises over four bars, using two or three notes of the scale and rhythmic ideas. Less is more: space and rhythm matter more than many notes.
study.source: Original jazz workshop written for this lesson; the blues form and scale are standard jazz materials.
